criteria_description:
Evaluation purpose relates to the following question: WHY -> "Why do we need this assessment?" (cf. Metaframework first steps) Different possible purposes, as described in Darmaun et al (2023): Localised steering, benchmarking, design an agroecological transition, advocacy. 
•	Localized steering: When the purpose of the evaluation is localized steering, it is highly contextualized and tailored to the specific farm, organisation, territory, or stakeholder network in which it is applied. Its aim is to generate practical information for monitoring progress, identifying challenges, coordinating stakeholders, and supporting decisions about how the agroecological transition should be managed and adjusted in that particular context.
•	Designing an agroecological transition: When the purpose is to design an agroecological transition, the evaluation is forward-looking and highly contextualized. It is used to explore possible transition pathways, define priorities and objectives, identify appropriate actions, anticipate potential barriers and trade-offs, and guide the development of strategies, interventions, or policies suited to the local context.
•	Benchmarking: When the purpose is benchmarking, the evaluation is structured to enable comparison with other farms, organisations, territories, or systems, or with predefined reference points. These reference points may include historical performance, policy targets, agreed sustainability thresholds, scientific standards, sectoral averages, or societally defined goals. Benchmarking helps identify relative strengths and weaknesses and assess progress towards a desired level of performance.
•	Advocacy: When the purpose is advocacy, the evaluation is designed to produce clear, credible, and communicable evidence that can convey a particular message, raise awareness, support a position, or persuade decision-makers and other stakeholders. The results may be used to influence public debate, justify policy change, mobilise resources, strengthen stakeholder claims, or build support for agroecological transitions.
criteria_examples: In case studies applying RISE, the auditors calculated the values of all indicators for the three dimensions of sustainability and then took the results back to each of the farmers to discuss the context-specific improvements that are possible and they can work on. So, in such a case, the purpose is "localised steering".
criteria_coded_values: Localised steering; benchmarking; design; advocacy

criteria_description: Level of Participation. In Darmaun et al. (2023), three stages of involvement were identified: 1) in the development of the method (or its adaptation), 2) in the use (implementation) of the method and 3) in an ex-post evaluation of the method. (4) No stakeholders, i.e. farmers, were involved, and the data is collected from a secondary source.
criteria_examples: If the farmers are involved in thinking on what should be assessed, with which indicators, according to which reference values etc., then they are involved in the development (or adaptation) of the method -> (1). If the farmers are mobilized to share information on their farm, i.e. data collection, then they are involved in the use (2). If results are shared with them and they are able to provide feedback on these then they are involved in the ex-post evaluation (3). (4) No stakeholders, i.e. farmers, were involved, and the data is collected from a secondary source.

criteria_description:
Different ways of adapting: 
•A0 : Measurement contextualisation -> Adapting the language, units, terminology and formulation of data-collection instruments to ensure local understanding and measurement equivalence, while preserving the original indicator set and meaning. Example: Translating the tool, converting units, rephrasing survey questions, adapting local terminology or examples. 
•A1 : Selection of original indicators-> Users select, remove or prioritise indicators from the original indicator set, without adding new indicators. Example: Only the indicators relevant to crop production are retained from the full tool
•A2 : Addition of localised indicators -> New indicators are searched for, developed or added to represent local conditions, priorities or practices. Example: Adding an indicator on water scarcity that was absent from the original tool. 
•A3 : Modification of tool structure (architecture of the tool) -> The original structure, dimensions, hierarchy, aggregation or organisation of the tool is changed. Example: Reorganising the tool into locally relevant way. 
•A4 : Modification of the way the tool is used (use of tool) -> The tool’s original procedures, data-collection methods, users, timing or application process are changed. Example: Replacing farm measurements with interviews, or applying the tool through participatory workshops. 
•A5 : Use of built-in flexibility -> The method is adapted using flexibility explicitly provided in its original design, without modifying the tool beyond its intended options. Example: This applies if the tool is mostly a guidance rather than a prescriptive handbook (e.g. MESMIS).
criteria_coded_values:
YES/ NO + A0 to A5 codes + add columns to provide detail (one with exact quotation from use case + another with our own words if needed): 
•A0 : Measurement contextualisation 
•A1 : Selection of original indicators 
•A2 : Addition of localised indicators 
•A3 : Modification of tool structure 
•A4 : Modification of the way the tool is used 
•A5 : Use of built-in flexibility

criteria_description:
Farm performance assessment means understanding how well a farm is doing by looking at a range of criteria and indicators, such as e.g. its productivity, profitability, environmental impact, and social outcomes. Raw results of the indicators (whether measured, calculated, observed, or reported) need to be interpreted (i.e. if the raw value is "good", "bad", etc.). To do this, they must be compared with reference values that illustrate target levels to be achieved or thresholds to be avoided (Lairez et al, 2015). Different types of reference values exist: absolute or relative (cf. Van Cauwenbergh et al. 2007; Lebacq et al., 2013; Lairez et al., 2015)
1) Absolute reference values: predefined based on scientific literature (e.g. irreversibility thresholds) or societal consensus, established through expert consultation (e.g. target values, regulatory standards)
2) Relative reference values: derived from comparisons, either across space, by comparing with other agroecosystems (e.g., regional averages) (i.e. values based on a comparable group), or over time, by comparing with an initial value of the evaluated agroecosystem (i.e. values based on trends)
criteria_coded_values:
YES/ NO (for consideration of performance assessment; "No" would mean that the case study does NOT consider the performance of the farm for social/economic/environemnt dimensions) + if YES also code the type of reference value used: 
•9 = No reference value used; indicators are reported but not evaluated against a benchmark
•1 = Absolute reference value 
•2 = Relative reference value—spatial comparison 
•3 = Relative reference value—temporal comparison 
•4 = Both absolute and relative reference values 
•5 = Unclear or not specified
+ add columns to provide detail (one with exact quotation from use case + another with our own words if needed)
